text:
Why Joined-Up Handwriting Still Belongs in Primary School

Every few years someone declares joined-up handwriting dead. The argument goes that children will spend their adult lives tapping on glass and pressing keys, so the hours spent practising loops and exit strokes are a sentimental throwback, like teaching them to churn butter. Finland stopped requiring cursive in 2016 and put keyboard skills in its place. The American Common Core standards dropped it in 2010. In staffrooms in England, where the national curriculum still expects pupils to join their letters by the end of Key Stage 2, some teachers quietly wonder whether the effort is worth it.

I think it is. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting. The reason has little to do with nostalgia or neat penmanship. Fluent handwriting is a working tool for thinking, and joining letters is how most children get fluent. If we drop it, we save a little classroom time and lose something much harder to get back.

**Writing by hand is still a large part of school**

Start with the plain practical case. Children in British schools do most of their written work by hand, from Year 1 through to the end of secondary school. GCSE and A-level exams are still overwhelmingly sat on paper. A sixteen-year-old writing an English Literature essay under timed conditions is in a race against the clock, and the speed of their hand sets a ceiling on what they can show. A pupil who prints each letter separately, lifting the pen between every stroke, is spending part of that time on movement instead of thought.

Joined writing is faster for most people once it is learned, because the pen stays on the page and each letter flows into the next. That matters less at seven than at sixteen, but the habits formed at seven are the ones that last. Handwriting is a motor skill, and like other motor skills it is easiest to shape early and hard to remodel later. A child who reaches secondary school with a slow, laboured print style rarely gets a second round of explicit teaching. Secondary teachers have content to cover; they are not going to stop a history lesson to work on letter formation.

The obvious reply is that exams will go digital, and some boards are moving that way. Perhaps they will. But "perhaps, eventually" is a weak basis for removing a skill from children who are in school now and will be sitting paper exams for the next decade. Even in a world of on-screen assessment, people still fill in forms, write notes in meetings, sign cards, label boxes and jot reminders. Handwriting has shrunk as a share of adult life, but it has not vanished, and the times when it is needed tend to be the times when no device is to hand.

**Handwriting helps children learn to read and write**

The stronger case concerns what handwriting does for learning itself. There is a good body of research suggesting that forming letters by hand helps young children recognise them and learn to spell. Studies by the psychologist Virginia Berninger and colleagues at the University of Washington found that primary-age children writing by hand tended to produce more words, more quickly, and to express more ideas than when they typed. Brain-imaging work with young children has found that practising letters by hand activates reading-related brain areas in ways that typing or tracing does not. More recently, EEG studies from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology have reported richer patterns of brain connectivity when students write by hand than when they type, which the researchers link to memory and learning.

None of this evidence is perfect, and it would be a mistake to overstate it. Some headline findings, such as the claim that students who take notes on laptops remember less than those who write by hand, have had mixed results when other researchers tried to replicate them. But the general direction of the research is consistent: the physical act of making letters seems to help children fix them in memory, and fluent handwriting frees up attention for composition. When a child no longer has to think about how to form a "b" or where the pen goes next, the mind is free to think about what the sentence should say.

That last point is the heart of the matter. Psychologists talk about "transcription" skills (handwriting and spelling) and "composition" skills (ideas, structure, vocabulary). In young writers the two compete for the same limited working memory. A child struggling with letter formation has less mental room left for ideas, so their writing comes out shorter and simpler than their thinking. Making handwriting automatic is how you clear that bottleneck, and teaching a consistent joined style with regular practice is the most reliable way schools have found to make it automatic.

**Joining makes spelling stick**

Joined-up writing has a particular advantage here. When letters are joined, common letter strings like "-ing", "-tion", "th" and "ou" become single, flowing movements. Many teachers and specialists believe this gives children a kind of physical memory for spelling patterns: the hand learns the shape of a word as one gesture. This is one reason some dyslexia specialists have long recommended a cursive style, arguing that it reduces confusion between letters such as "b" and "d", since each letter starts from the line and has a distinct movement. The evidence on this is more practical experience than controlled trial, and not every expert agrees. Still, it is a reasonable idea backed by a lot of classroom experience, and it points the same way as the wider research on handwriting and literacy.

**The case against, taken seriously**

The arguments against teaching joined writing deserve a fair hearing, because some of them are good.

The first is time. The primary curriculum is crowded, and every hour spent on handwriting practice is an hour not spent on something else. But handwriting practice is cheap. Ten or fifteen minutes a few times a week in the early years is enough to build the habit, and much of that practice can be combined with spelling and phonics. Weighed against the hours that slow, effortful writing costs a child over the next ten years of school, it is a good trade.

The second is that print is perfectly adequate. Plenty of adults print and get on fine. This is true, and it should shape how joined writing is taught. Nobody needs to produce the ornate copperplate of a Victorian clerk, and schools that mark children down for an unconventional join are missing the point. The goal is fast, legible writing. Many adults end up with a hybrid style, joining some letters and not others, and that is fine. But a hybrid style usually grows out of having been taught to join in the first place. Children who are only ever taught print rarely discover joins on their own; they just print, slowly.

The third objection is the most important: some children find joined writing very hard. Children with dyspraxia, dysgraphia or other motor difficulties can be distressed by the demands of a cursive style, and forcing it on them can do harm. The answer here is flexibility. Good schools already make exceptions, allow some pupils to use print or a laptop, and provide occupational therapy support where needed. A sensible policy teaches joined writing as the default and adapts for children who need something else. Having exceptions does not show the rule is wrong; it shows the rule is being applied with judgement.

The fourth objection is that keyboards are the future, so schools should teach typing instead. This presents a false choice. Children should learn to type, and in many British primary schools typing is taught far too little. But typing and handwriting do different jobs. Typing is good for producing finished, editable text. Handwriting is good for thinking on paper: sketching a plan, annotating a text, working through a maths problem, writing notes in a margin. A good primary education teaches both, and there is no reason the case for one has to be made at the expense of the other.

**What the countries that dropped it learned**

It is worth looking at what happened where cursive was abandoned. In the United States, the removal of cursive from the Common Core standards was followed, over the next decade, by a steady stream of states putting it back. Over twenty states now require it in some form, and California passed a law in 2023 requiring cursive teaching in elementary schools. Some of that backlash was nostalgic, and some was about children being unable to read handwritten documents, including letters from their grandparents and historical sources. But a good part of it came from teachers and researchers who saw the effect on children's writing fluency and wanted it reversed. When a reform is undone this widely by people who watched it happen, that is worth noticing.

**A skill worth keeping**

Joined-up handwriting is not sacred. If it truly held children back, or if there were strong evidence that dropping it improved their learning, we should drop it without regret. But the evidence points the other way. Handwriting fluency supports reading, spelling and composition. Joining is the most common route to fluency. Children still write by hand for most of their schooling and will sit paper exams for years to come. The costs of teaching it are small, and they can be reduced further with flexible teaching and sensible exceptions for children who struggle.

The real question is whether we want children's hands to keep up with their minds. Teaching a fluent, joined style in the primary years is one of the simplest ways to make sure they do. Schools should keep teaching it, teach it well, and stop apologising for it.
